paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Lockett took place in Atlanta, Georgia, on the afternoon of July 13, 1903, when a large crowd gathered at a house on Central Street where Lockett, a Black man, had been seized after being accused of attacking Mrs. Susie Wells. Despite "many threats of lynching," patrolmen removed Lockett by a back street and lodged him in the Tower. The incident is known from a single telegraph dispatch printed in the New-York Tribune under the headline "Negro Saved from Atlanta Mob."

According to the Atlanta dispatch, Lockett attacked Mrs. Susie Wells at her home on Central Street that afternoon; the dispatch does not describe the nature of the alleged attack. Her screams brought her sons, who overpowered Lockett "after a hard fight." News of the affair spread through the city, and by the time officers arrived a large crowd had collected about the house.

Members of the crowd made "many threats of lynching," but the patrolmen took Lockett away by a back street and "landed him safely in the Tower." The dispatch gives neither the size nor the composition of the crowd, and it reports no injuries to Lockett from the crowd.

The dispatch closed with the remark that "it is believed that Lockett is partially insane." No report of a charge, trial, or later disposition of Lockett's case appears in the coverage, and no arrests of members of the crowd were reported.

The only located account is a brief item "by telegraph to the Tribune" that ran in the New-York Tribune on July 14, 1903. Its headline cast the patrolmen as having "saved" Lockett from a "mob," while the text stated the attack on Mrs. Wells as fact rather than as an accusation and identified Lockett only as "a negro." The item offered no comment on the crowd's threats beyond reporting them, and it ended by suggesting Lockett was mentally unsound.
No coverage of the incident in Atlanta papers or in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Lockett
bases: A crowd gathered at the house where Lockett was held and made 'many threats of lynching' before patrolmen removed him to the Tower, a threatened lynching (A1).

Lockett was not killed: the only report says patrolmen got him away from a threatening crowd and 'landed him safely in the Tower' (A1); the crowd's threats were extralegal and tied to the accusation, but no one was killed.
One telegraph dispatch printed in the New-York Tribune (A1) is the only report found; no Atlanta, other white, or Black-press account was located.

accounts.label: Atlanta telegraph dispatch
accounts.gist: Lockett attacked Mrs. Wells, was overpowered by her sons, and was saved from a threatening crowd by patrolmen who took him to the Tower; he was believed partially insane.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined the item 'NEGRO SAVED FROM ATLANTA MOB', presented the accusation as fact, and closed with the belief that Lockett was 'partially insane'; it neither condemns nor endorses the crowd.

record_check.record: After a Black man, Charles Lockett, was held at Mrs. Susie Wells's home for an alleged attack...
record_check.dossier: The dispatch says Wells's sons overpowered Lockett after a hard fight and the crowd collected about the house before officers arrived; 'held at her home' is an inference, and the attack is stated by the dispatch, not established.
Held by Wells's sons, then taken by patrolmen to the Tower; never taken by the crowd
The threats followed the accusation that Lockett attacked Mrs. Wells

info: Afternoon of July 13, 1903 (dispatch dated Atlanta, July 13, says 'this afternoon')
Home of Mrs. Susie Wells, Central Street, Atlanta
Charles Lockett, described as 'a negro'; threatened with lynching, not harmed by the crowd as reported
Accused of attacking Mrs. Susie Wells at her home; the nature of the attack is not stated
A 'large crowd' of unstated size and unstated race

sources.note: Telegraph dispatch dated Atlanta, July 13: Lockett accused of attacking Mrs. Susie Wells, overpowered by her sons; crowd made 'many threats of lynching'; patrolmen took him by a back street to the Tower.
quotes: Mrs. Susie Wells was attacked at her home in Central-st. this afternoon by Charles Lockett, a negro.
There were many threats of lynching, but the patrolmen got the negro away by a back street and landed him safely in the Tower.
It is believed that Lockett is partially insane.
